name: Hallstatt
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.

attributes.attribute: archaeological site on a salt mountain over Lake Hallstatt in the Upper Austrian Alps
type-site and namesake of the Hallstatt Iron Age culture, so called since the late 19th century
early excavations at the graveyard led by Georg Ramsauer
about 2000 burials, some 1270 recovered, roughly 45 percent cremations
graves date mainly to Hallstatt C and D, c. 750-475 bc
rich bronze vessels and metal goods mark high-ranking burials; new estimates suggest 5000-8000 graves
mining on the Hallstatt mountain began in the Late Bronze Age, 12th/11th century bc
deepest shaft reached 215 metres; a landslide around 350 bc ended local mining
material found from France to eastern Hungary and southern Germany to Slovenia
divided into a west and an east zone near the rivers Inn, Enns, and Moldau
dated about 750-475/450 bc via southern Mediterranean imports
later phases linked by scholars to the ethnic label Celts
Greek colony, present-day Marseille, founded c. 600 bc, a node of the Mediterranean trade

text: Hallstatt is a salt-mining town set above a lake in the Austrian Alps. The place gives its name to the first culture plainly read as Celtic. Crews dug the mines on a wide scale between 1846 and 1899. The culture moved through four named stages, A through D. Those stages stretch from about 1200 bc to about 600 bc. Across much of Europe its effect ran from roughly 800 bc to 450 bc. It replaced the earlier Umfield culture and gave way later to La Tene. Hallstatt art is mostly straight-edged and geometric in form. Crafters valued it for skill more than for beauty. The bird picture may have come from Italy, while plant shapes stay scarce.

okr.objective: Document Hallstatt as both an Upper Austrian salt-mining graveyard and the type culture of the early Celtic Iron Age in central Europe.
key_results: Describe the site, its cemetery, and the prehistoric salt mines and their dating.
Explain the Hallstatt culture's territory, east-west division, and chronology.
Note its ties to the Celts and to Mediterranean trade.
